name: Map scale and distance
subject: Geography
example_problem: The distance between two points on a 1:50 000 topographic map is 8,6 cm. Calculate the real distance in kilometres.
prior_knowledge: Student knows ratio scale and metric unit conversions

importance.summary: Scale and distance calculations sit inside Mapwork Question 3 on BOTH papers (30/150 each, Gr 11 and Gr 12 - calculations are 10 of those 30 marks) and inside development and climate topics' integrated mapwork.

required_by.topic: Subtropical anticyclones and associated weather conditions

covered_by.topic: Consolidation of Grade 8 and 9 map skills
covered_by.subtopic: Scale and measuring distance (line and ratio scales); coordinates to locate features

diagnostic.prompt: Two points are 8,6 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map. The real distance is:
On a 1:50 000 sheet, one centimetre of map represents:

recap:
The ratio scale 1:50 000 means one unit of any length on the map represents 50 000 of the same units on the ground. It is unitless - measure in centimetres and multiply by 50 000, and the answer is in centimetres of real ground. Feel the size: 50 000 cm is 500 m, so every map centimetre is half a kilometre; two centimetres, one kilometre.

The standard calculation, four lines. One: measure (or receive) the map distance - point-centre to point-centre, to the nearest millimetre; at this scale each millimetre of sloppiness is 50 m of ground. Two: multiply by the scale factor - 8,6 cm × 50 000 = 430 000 cm. Three: walk the metric ladder - divide by 100 for metres (4 300 m), divide by 1 000 for kilometres (4,3 km). Four: state the answer WITH its unit, in the unit the question demands. The ladder chant: centi to metres, divide by a hundred; metres to kays, divide by a thousand.

Curved distances - a winding road or river - defeat a rigid ruler: lay a string or paper-strip edge along the bends, mark the end, straighten it against the ruler, and read the total map distance; the arithmetic afterwards is identical. Memos accept a small range on curved measurements, so press the string into every bend rather than cutting corners.

Different scale, same machine: on a 1:10 000 orthophoto, multiply by 10 000 instead - 8,6 cm is only 0,86 km. Never assume the scale; read it off the sheet, especially when a question moves between the topographic map and the orthophoto. And remember which is the LARGER scale: 1:10 000, because one ten-thousandth is the bigger fraction - larger scale, smaller area, more detail. The reverse question runs the machine backwards: real distance to map distance means convert to centimetres, then DIVIDE by the scale factor - 4,3 km = 430 000 cm ÷ 50 000 = 8,6 cm.

The sense check that saves matrics: about 10 cm on a 1:50 000 sheet is 5 km. If 8,6 cm produces 43 km or 0,43 km, a decimal slipped on the ladder. Convert, then ask whether you could walk the answer in an afternoon.

exit_check.prompt: The metric ladder from centimetres to kilometres runs:
To measure distance along a winding river on the map, you should:
options: Lay string or a paper strip along the bends, straighten it, and read against a ruler
Measure the straight line between endpoints

exit_check.prompt: Which map has the larger scale, and what does that mean?
options: 1:10 000 - a bigger fraction, showing a smaller area in more detail

exit_check.prompt: The real distance is 4,3 km. On a 1:50 000 map the points are apart by:
options: 8,6 cm - convert to 430 000 cm and divide by 50 000
